name: Deep Space 1
significance: Deep Space 1 was NASA's first New Millennium Program mission and, above all, an engineering proving ground: it was the first spacecraft to use ion propulsion as its primary means of propulsion rather than for minor station-keeping, and it validated eleven other new technologies in flight, including autonomous optical navigation, a solar-concentrator array, and miniaturized instruments. Its NSTAR ion engine, thrusting almost continuously for years rather than in one chemical-rocket burst, set a record for total velocity change generated by a spacecraft's own propulsion, proving the technology later relied on by Dawn, Hayabusa, Hayabusa2, and BepiColombo. Its lone primary science target, the small asteroid 9969 Braille, was mostly an engineering-test casualty -- a navigation-software glitch left the spacecraft 26 km rather than the planned 240 m away -- but the extended mission's flyby of comet 19P/Borrelly redeemed the science return, capturing the highest-resolution comet-nucleus images obtained up to that time and revealing an elongated, jet-active nucleus. In short, DS1 de-risked ion propulsion and autonomous deep-space navigation for every subsequent low-thrust mission that followed it.
statusNote: Continuous NSTAR ion-engine thrust throughout the cruise, not ballistic coasting, the same modeling caveat as Dawn/Hayabusa/Hayabusa2/BepiColombo -- each leg here is a smooth Lambert arc anchored to the real recorded encounter dates, approximating the shape of a continuous low-thrust trajectory rather than a literal coast. No gravity assists; the entire Earth->Braille->Borrelly path was shaped purely by the ion engine. The planned 9969 Braille encounter (1999-07-29) was meant to pass within 240 m, but an AutoNav targeting fault left the actual closest approach at roughly 26 km. The extended-mission flyby of comet 19P/Borrelly (2001-09-22, closest approach 2,171 km) was the mission's primary scientific return.
